sources.h1: MXR Bass Overdrive M89 Review — Warm Grit That Cuts Through a Mix
sources.excerpt: MXR Bass Overdrive M89 Review: Grit That Cuts Through Skip to content Play Bass Better Menu Courses About Blog Connect Search for: Search Search Search for: Search MXR Bass Overdrive M89 Review — Warm Grit That Cuts Through a Mix Scroll MXR Bass Overdrive M89 Review — Warm Grit That Cuts Through a Mix Bass overdrive is a topic that splits players right down the middle. Half want something that sounds like a slightly cranked amp — warm, organic, responsive. The other half want something with character and grit that sits in a band mix without disappearing. The MXR Bass Overdrive M89 tries to be both. I’ve been running this pedal in my signal chain for a while now and I have thoughts. Not all of them positive, but overall the M89 has earned its spot on my board in certain contexts. What the M89 Is Designed to Do The M89 is a bass-specific overdrive — not a guitar overdrive with a bass blend knob bolted on, which is what a lot of “bass overdrive” pedals actually are. MXR built this one from the ground up for low frequencies. The circuit is designed to preserve low-end content while adding harmonic saturation to the midrange and upper frequencies. The controls are simple: Drive, Tone, Output. Three knobs. No dry blend, no EQ bands, no extra voicing switches. That simplicity is either a feature or a limitation depending on what you’re looking for. There’s also a Gate control — a noise gate built into the pedal — which is genuinely useful if you’re running single-coil pickups or playing in a noisy venue. Tone Character — What It Actually Sounds Like At low drive settings the M89 adds a gentle warmth and a slight compression that makes the bass feel more present in a mix. It’s not dramatic — you could argue it sounds like running through a good tube preamp rather than an overdrive pedal. That’s the sweet spot for players who want “something” without obviously sounding like they’re using a dirt pedal. Push the drive past noon and the harmonic saturation becomes more pronounced. The mids get pushed forward, the attack gets slightly compressed, and you start to hear that gritty texture on note attacks. It’s controlled — never spiky or harsh. But it’s clearly overdrive territory now. Full drive is where it gets aggressive. The low end holds together better than I expected — most overdrive pedals fall apart in the bottom end at high gain. The M89 maintains definition even when cranked, though at full drive the tone starts to feel slightly compressed and one-dimensional. Most useful settings are in the first two thirds of the drive control’s range. The Tone knob is effective but sweeps a fairly narrow range. It does what it says but don’t expect massive tonal shaping from it. Think of it as a presence adjustment rather than a full EQ control. How It Sits in a Band Mix This is where the M89 either justifies itself or doesn’t. I’ve used it on stage and in studio sessions, and my honest assessment is: it works better live than in isolation. Alone in a bedroom it can sound slightly compressed and midrange-heavy. That’s a characteristic of the circuit that becomes an advantage in a band context. Those pushed mids cut through guitars and keys without needing a separate boost. The low end stays thick enough to hold down the foundation. You remain audible and defined without having to fight for space in the frequency spectrum. For rock, soul, R&B with edge — the M89 is a solid working-musician choice. It does its job without drama. The Gate Feature I’ll be honest — I didn’t expect to like the built-in gate. Gates on dirt pedals often feel tacked on and cause more problems than they solve, cutting sustain unnaturally or opening too slowly. The M89’s gate is better than average. At moderate settings it cleans up noise between notes without choking sustain. For live playing where stage noise is a factor this is genuinely useful.
